headline: Employment Relations Bill Advances Amid Dispute Over Contractor Status and Worker Rights
summary: Parliament’s extended sitting was dominated by debate over the Employment Relations Amendment Bill, which would change how some workers are classified and alter access to personal grievance claims and collective agreements. Opposition MPs warned the changes could weaken protections, particularly for contractors and vulnerable workers, while the Government said they would give businesses greater certainty and flexibility. Question time and the Prime Minister’s statement debate also exposed divisions over electricity costs, unemployment, poverty, public services and foreign policy.

topicSummaries.topic: Employment Relations Bill Advances Despite Worker-Protection Concerns
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: The proposed changes could affect access to paid leave, personal grievance claims and collective agreements for workers whose status is disputed.
topicSummaries.content: The House committee considered major changes to the Employment Relations Act, including a gateway test for classifying specified contractors, limits on personal grievance remedies in cases involving employee misconduct or contribution, a $200,000 remuneration threshold for some dismissal claims, and repeal of the 30-day rule that currently keeps new workers covered by a collective agreement initially. Labour and Green MPs warned the changes could make it easier to classify employees as contractors and reduce workplace protections; Workplace Relations Minister Brooke van Velden said the gateway test includes written-agreement, availability and other criteria, and that existing tests can still apply where the criteria are not met. The committee rejected opposition amendments and approved the main provisions and a government transitional amendment. After further debate on Thursday morning, the bill was reported with amendment; it had not completed its remaining parliamentary stages.

keyExchanges.speaker: Helen White (Labour)
keyExchanges.quote: How is the Minister going to protect that person under this law, where they are simply signing up that they’re specified to be a contractor but, in fact, they’ll be subject to great exploitation?

keyExchanges.speaker: Brooke van Velden (ACT)
keyExchanges.quote: If those gateway criteria are not met, then the current section 6 actually still applies, so employees can still challenge their status based on the existing test if any of those criteria are not met.

topicSummaries.topic: Parties Clash Over LNG Levy and Promised Power-Bill Savings
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: The dispute concerns who may ultimately pay for a proposed LNG backup facility and whether it will lower household and business electricity bills.
topicSummaries.content: Prime Minister Christopher Luxon and Energy Minister Simon Watts defended a proposed liquefied natural gas import facility as backup electricity supply for dry years, saying it was expected to reduce power prices. Labour questioned whether a charge on electricity companies would be passed on to consumers and challenged the Government’s projected savings, which Luxon put at about $50 a year for an average household. Watts said the levy would be on the electricity sector and cited advice that lower electricity prices were expected to more than offset the cost. The exchange did not resolve questions about how savings would be passed through to consumers or the market conditions affecting bills.

keyExchanges.speaker: Chris Hipkins (Labour)
keyExchanges.quote: Is it a tax, a levy, a fee, or a charge?

keyExchanges.speaker: Christopher Luxon (National)
keyExchanges.quote: What it is is lower power bills for New Zealanders.

topicSummaries.topic: Unemployment and Material Hardship Fuel Cost-of-Living Debate
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: Jobs, food prices and hardship support affect household budgets and the ability of families to meet basic needs.
topicSummaries.content: Labour MPs used the Salvation Army’s State of the Nation report and labour-market figures to argue that unemployment, child poverty and material hardship were worsening, with particular concern raised about Māori, Pasifika and disabled people. Labour speakers also cited rising supermarket costs and described housing insecurity in their electorates. Finance Minister Nicola Willis acknowledged that 156,000 children were reported to be living in material hardship, while pointing to Working for Families, tax relief and other support; Social Development Minister Louise Upston cited 15,000 additional people in work in the December quarter and said other labour-market indicators were improving. The competing accounts reflected a wider dispute over whether economic conditions were improving and who was benefiting.

keyExchanges.speaker: Barbara Edmonds (Labour)
keyExchanges.quote: Are 156,000 children living in material hardship, as reported by the Salvation Army, a sign of a growing economy?

keyExchanges.speaker: Nicola Willis (National)
keyExchanges.quote: No. However, what I would say is that there would be more children who would be experiencing material hardship if it were not for this Government’s decisive measures

topicSummaries.topic: Finance Minister Orders Independent Review of Reserve Bank’s COVID Response
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: The review will examine decisions made during the pandemic that the Government links to inflation, house prices and public costs, informing how future economic shocks are handled.
topicSummaries.content: Finance Minister Nicola Willis announced an independent review of the Reserve Bank’s monetary-policy response to COVID-19, covering Monetary Policy Committee decisions and the analysis supporting them. She cited the official cash rate being cut to 0.25 percent, the Large Scale Asset Purchase programme, an estimated $10.3 billion in programme losses and a sharp rise in house prices, while acknowledging the measures helped preserve jobs and businesses. The review will also consider coordination and information-sharing between the Reserve Bank and Treasury, but not the wider fiscal response specifically. Labour MP Ingrid Leary criticised the announcement as a political distraction from current economic pressures; the review’s findings were not yet available.

keyExchanges.speaker: Nicola Willis (National)
keyExchanges.quote: The purpose of the review is to learn from experience so that future shocks can be navigated in the best possible way.

keyExchanges.speaker: Ingrid Leary (Labour)
keyExchanges.quote: This is a classic distraction. It is a classic smokescreen.

topicSummaries.topic: Anzac Day Bill Broadens Who Can Be Commemorated
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: The change expands formal recognition at Anzac Day services to people whose service or sacrifice was not clearly covered by the existing law.
topicSummaries.content: The committee approved the Anzac Day Amendment Bill without amendment. The bill broadens the categories of service recognised at Anzac Day commemorations, including peacekeeping, service connected with warlike conflicts, deaths during training and contributions beyond military uniformed service. Veterans Minister Chris Penk said the wording was intended to include New Zealanders who served under allied forces, while maintaining Anzac Day’s historical meaning. MPs noted that the bill changes commemoration rather than veterans’ financial entitlements, and that communities would continue to shape local ceremonies.

keyExchanges.speaker: Andy Foster (New Zealand First)
keyExchanges.quote: We need to be able to go to Anzac Day and say if we are recognising him, if we are recognising all of these people, that they are explicitly included.

keyExchanges.speaker: Chris Penk (National)
keyExchanges.quote: To me, the service of New Zealand very unambiguously does include those who are serving under a different banner

topicSummaries.topic: Public Service Bill Debate Raises Questions About Neutrality and Long-Term Duties
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: Changes to the Public Service Act could shape how senior officials serve governments, maintain neutrality and plan public services over time.
topicSummaries.content: The committee began consideration of the Public Service Amendment Bill, which the Government said would clarify chief executives’ responsibilities, strengthen performance management and improve value for money while retaining political neutrality and merit-based appointments. Labour MPs criticised the lack of cross-party consultation on changes to the Act’s purpose and raised concerns about removing references to active citizenship and long-term public interest. Minister James Meager said the spirit of service would remain in the purpose clause, with long-term responsibilities reflected elsewhere, and said ministerial responsibilities were better addressed through constitutional conventions and the Cabinet Manual. The committee reported progress rather than completing consideration of the bill.

keyExchanges.speaker: Helen White (Labour)
keyExchanges.quote: How, now, should the Public Service feel about their obligation under this new definition to look long term, to look to future Governments, etc., in their role?

keyExchanges.speaker: James Meager (National)
keyExchanges.quote: Our chief executives will be required to provide advice on the long-term implications of policies

topicSummaries.topic: Foreign Policy Debate Pits Cautious Diplomacy Against Calls for Clearer Positions
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: The debate concerns how New Zealand responds to international conflicts and human-rights issues, affecting the country’s diplomatic standing and relationships.
topicSummaries.content: Foreign Minister Winston Peters defended the Government’s approach as active but cautious diplomacy, citing extensive overseas engagement and support for reforming the United Nations. Labour MP Vanushi Walters argued that the Government’s positions on issues including Palestine, the Golan Heights and Iran represented a retreat from a consistent, values-based foreign policy. Their arguments formed part of a broader political clash over whether New Zealand should speak more forcefully on international events or prioritise measured diplomacy and national interests.

keyExchanges.speaker: Winston Peters (New Zealand First)
keyExchanges.quote: We choose to do this calmly and rationally, as realists via diplomacy.

keyExchanges.speaker: Vanushi Walters (Labour)
keyExchanges.quote: We have gone from solidarity to silence and from silence to strangeness.

conclusion: The Government advanced major changes to employment law, but disputes over worker protections, household pressures and the direction of public policy remained unresolved.
